rules.title: No statewide rent control; rent increases must not be unconscionable
rules.requirement: New Jersey has no state law that caps or controls rent, but municipalities may pass local rent control or rent-leveling ordinances. Where no local ordinance applies, a landlord may raise rent only by terminating the old lease and offering a new lease at the increased rate, and the increase must not be unconscionable (so unreasonable as to shock the conscience).
rules.exemptions: Rents subject to a municipal rent control ordinance are governed by that ordinance instead. Newly constructed multiple dwellings and government-subsidized, HUD-insured, or NJHMFA-financed housing may be exempt from local rent control ordinances.
rules.interaction: Unconscionability is assessed case-by-case considering the size of the increase, landlord's expenses/profitability, comparable rents, bargaining position, and judicial discretion (Fromet Properties v. Buel; Hale v. Farrakhan). Local rent control/leveling ordinances, where enacted, take precedence over this general standard.
rules.quoted_span: Although the State of New Jersey does not have any laws that establish, govern, or control rents, a landlord can increase rents if they follow certain procedures.

rules.title: Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law - 30-year exemption from local rent control
rules.requirement: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinance for 30 years following completion of construction of the building.

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to newly constructed multiple dwellings; the exemption runs for 30 years from completion of construction.

rules.interaction: Rents subsidized by governmental funding may also be exempt from local rent control ordinances.
rules.quoted_span: newly constructed multiple dwellings shall be exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction of the building

rules.title: No rent increase to cover condominium/cooperative conversion costs
rules.requirement: If a building is converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. This prohibition applies to all tenants in the building regardless of protected-tenancy status.
rules.exemptions: Rents may still be increased to cover the cost of new services or amenities.
rules.quoted_span: rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the conversion

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act notice-to-quit requirement before eviction for nonpayment of an increased rent
rules.requirement: Before a landlord can evict a tenant for nonpayment of an increased rent, the landlord must first serve the tenant with a valid notice to quit and notice of rent increase. The tenant need not leave and may remain as long as they pay any legal rent increase.
rules.interaction: If a tenant disputes the increase as unconscionable and withholds payment, the landlord may file an eviction action for nonpayment and a judge decides whether the increase was unconscionable; if not unconscionable, the tenant must pay it to avoid eviction.
rules.quoted_span: before an owner can evict a tenant for nonpayment of an increased rent, they must first serve the tenant with a valid notice to quit and notice of rent increase

rules.title: Landlord registration required before a tenant may be evicted
rules.requirement: A landlord must file a registration statement (with the municipal clerk for one- or two-family non-owner-occupied homes, or with the Bureau of Housing Inspection for buildings with three or more units). A landlord who has not properly registered is barred from evicting a tenant from the building.

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to non-owner-occupied one- or two-family homes and to buildings with three or more rental units.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two-family homes are not required to be registered.
rules.interaction: If a landlord has failed to register, the court must reserve judgment and continue an eviction case for up to 90 days to allow time to comply; if the landlord still has not complied, the case must be dismissed.
rules.quoted_span: The landlord registration law prohibits a landlord from evicting a tenant in the building if the landlord has not been properly registered

rules.title: Security deposit must be returned within 30 days of tenancy termination
rules.requirement: Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest earned, less lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear and tear or other money owed under the lease, sent by personal delivery, registered, or certified mail along with an itemized list of any deductions.
rules.exemptions: No deductions may be made from the security deposit of a tenant who remains in possession of the rental premises. A shortened 5-business-day return period applies when a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation, or evacuation.
rules.interaction: Interest earned on the deposit must separately be paid or credited to the tenant under N.J.S.A. 46:8-19(c); failure to pay required interest or give notice lets the tenant apply the deposit plus 7% annual interest toward rent under N.J.S.A. 46:8-19.1(c).
rules.penalty: If the landlord fails to timely return the deposit, or the tenant disputes a deduction, the tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.
rules.quoted_span: Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination bars tenant screening based on source of lawful income
rules.requirement: Landlords and rental agencies may not refuse to rent to, or otherwise discriminate against, prospective tenants based on source of lawful income (such as housing vouchers or public assistance), along with race, creed, color, national origin, sex, marital status, familial status, disability, and other protected categories.

coverage_conditions.notes: Exempt: two-family owner-occupied dwellings; rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home; single-sex residences as to familial status only.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply to two-family owner-occupied dwellings, rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, or residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex (e.g., YMCA, age-restricted housing), as it pertains to familial status.
rules.interaction: A landlord may still lawfully refuse an applicant for insufficient income, overcrowding that would violate zoning, or poor credit history under 42 U.S.C.A. §§ 3601-3610; violations of the Law Against Discrimination can result in fines up to $10,000 for a first offense under N.J.S.A. 10:5-14.1a(a).
rules.penalty: Up to $10,000 for a first offense, plus potential monetary damages and an order to rent the unit to the complainant.
rules.quoted_span: requires equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender  identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income
